title: Anamniocentesis: parthenogenesis testing of oviparous embryos from perivitelline fluid
content:
Abstract
Conservation efforts aiming to rewild the endangered zebra shark using aquarium broodstock are challenged by parthenogenesis, a reproductive phenomenon where embryos develop without male genetic input. As parthenogenetic offspring are genetically inbred and have low survival rates post-hatch, their removal from the pool of reintroduced animals would enable efficient use of conservation resources. We explored whether genetic testing of the perivitelline fluid surrounding developing embryos could be used to detect parthenotes. Initial testing demonstrated that females did not impart a maternal signal on egg fluid, and fluid from eggs with postmortem embryos (positive controls) had good detection frequencies (82%). However, fluid from eggs with live embryos had decreased detection frequencies and fewer amplified loci (64% vs 82%; median loci #: 10 vs 4). Imaging cytometry of egg fluid from postmortem embryos revealed abundant shed cells in contrast to the dearth of cells in egg fluid from live embryos, providing a biological underpinning to the reduced power to genetically detect parthenotes. Scanning electron microscopy of postmortem embryos revealed sloughing and swollen epithelial cells in contrast to the smooth and continuous epithelium of live embryos. Results indicate that anamniocentesis-like methods can be used to genetically determine parentage prior to hatching.
